text.p: Following are some of the major events to have occurred on August 18 in history:
1559 - Pope Paul IV, pope from 1555 to 1559, died. The main feature of his pontificate was his implacable opposition to Spain, renewing the war between France and the Habsburgs.
1587 - Virginia Dare became the first child of English parents to be born in America. She, and the rest of the early settlement at Roanoke, later disappeared without trace.
1743 - The first rules of boxing were approved; they were drafted by John Broughton, third heavyweight boxing champion of England.
1759 - A French fleet was destroyed at Lagos, Portugal, by the British under Admiral Boscawen.
1765 - Holy Roman Emperor Francis I died; his eldest son became emperor as Josef II.
1774 - Meriwether Lewis, U.S. explorer, born. He led an expedition in 1804 to explore the unknown lands west of the Mississippi to the Pacific.
1792 - John Russell, 1st Earl Russell, British prime minister 1846-52 and 1865-66, born; champion of the Parliamentary Reform Bill of 1832.
1807 - Charles Francis Adams, U.S. statesman and economist, born. Son of President John Quincy Adams, he was ambassador to Britain 1861-68.
1825 - Scottish explorer Alexander Gordon Laing became the first European to reach Timbuktu, now in Mali. He was murdered there the following month.
1830 - Francis Joseph I, Emperor of Austria-Hungary, born. He was father of Archduke Francis Ferdinand whose assassination in 1914 precipitated World War One.
1862 - The Sioux Indians began an uprising in Minnesota; it was later crushed.
1870 - A major battle of the Franco-Prussian war took place at Gravelotte where the French were defeated; over 30,000 died.

1900 - Vijaya Lakshmi Pandit, Indian politician and diplomat and one of the world's leading women of the time, born. She served as ambassador to Moscow, Washington and Mexico and was the President of the U.N. General Assembly in 1953.
1908 - Edgar Faure, French politician and prime minister in 1952 and 1955-56, born. He represented France at the Nuremberg war trials after World War Two.
1917 - Casper Weinberger, U.S. politician who served under Presidents Nixon and Ford and was defence secretary under Reagan, born.
1922 - Shelley Winters, U.S. actress, born. She appeared in many films from 1943 including "A Double Life", "A Patch of Blue" and "The Diary of Anne Frank".
1933 - Roman Polanski, film director, born in Paris of Polish parents; directed films such as "Knife in the Water", "Rosemary's Baby" and "Chinatown".
1937 - Robert Redford, U.S. actor, born. Starred in films such as "Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid", "The Sting" and "All the President's Men".
1932 - Scottish aviator Jim Mollison made the first westbound transatlantic solo flight, from Portmarnock, Ireland, to Pennfield, New Brunswick.
1954 - James E. Wilkins became the first black to attend a U.S. cabinet meeting. He was Assistant Secretary of Labour and attended because the Secretary and Under-Secretary were away.
1960 - The first commercially-produced oral contraceptive, Enovid 10, was launched in Skokie, Illinois.
1964 - South Africa banned from the Olympic Games because of its apartheid policies.

1976 - Two American soldiers were killed by North Korean soldiers in a skirmish in the Joint Security Area in Panmunjom. Both sides immediately placed their forces on a state of war-readiness but the situation was resolved.
1989 - Colombian presidential candidate Luis Carlos Galan assassinated.
1990 - British warships were authorised to use force to enforce U.N. sanctions against Iraq. U.S. frigates fired warning shots for the first time across bows of two Iraqi tankers.
1993 - The U.S. told Sudan that it had been placed on the list of nations accused of sponsoring terrorism.
1994 - More than 120 people were killed by an earthquake measuring 5.6 on the Richter scale which struck in the Mascara region of western Algeria.
